Work from the project root, the main folder of the course. Read each step before you run its R chunk. All data are simulated. These exercises cannot show a finding about a real disease.

The [glossary](../docs/glossary.md) explains the course words. Each module reads its input files from disk. You do not need a saved R workspace.

```{r knit_setup, include=FALSE}
start_dir <- setwd(if (file.exists("config.R")) "." else "..")
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = getwd())
setwd(start_dir)
```

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("R/guided.R")
cfg <- guided_init()
```

## Module 6 at a glance {#module-6-overview}

**What you will do.** You will test one genetic variant by hand, then test all variants with a statistical model. You will read the output, check a rare variant and save the results in a standard file.

**What you will learn.**

- How to calculate an [odds ratio](../docs/glossary.md#or) from a simple table.
- How a model adjusts the comparison for [covariates](../docs/glossary.md#covariate), such as age.
- How to read one row of an [association](../docs/glossary.md#association) result.
- Why a rare variant needs [Firth correction](../docs/glossary.md#firth-regression).
- How to build a [summary statistics](../docs/glossary.md#summary-statistics) file that you can share.

**How long it takes.** About 60 minutes. The slowest step is 6.4, where PLINK tests every variant.

## 6.1 One variant by hand {#step-6-1}

### What we do

Calculate a simple carrier odds ratio for one variant on an [autosome](../docs/glossary.md#autosome) (a non-sex chromosome). The variant passed all quality control.

### Why

The [odds](../docs/glossary.md#odds) of an outcome are the number of people with the outcome divided by the number without it. An odds ratio (OR) compares the odds in two groups. An OR of 1 means the odds are equal. A carrier has at least one copy of an [allele](../docs/glossary.md#allele) (one version of the variant). We compare carriers of the allele named in the exported column with non-carriers. This is a teaching calculation. It is not the additive, adjusted model that the real GWAS uses. The counted allele matters: if you count the other allele, the contrast changes.

### You need

The full cohort from 5.7 and the retained variant 9:96426973:A:G.

### Command

```{r s6-1}
report <- guided_path(cfg, "6.1", "example")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--snp", "9:96426973:A:G", "--export", "A", "--out", report))
x <- read.table(paste0(report, ".raw"), header = TRUE, check.names = FALSE)
dose <- as.numeric(x[[7]])
psam <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), ".psam"))
case <- psam$Disease[match(x$IID, psam$IID)] == "2"
tab <- table(case = case, carrier = dose > 0)
print(tab)
carrier_or <- tab["TRUE", "TRUE"] * tab["FALSE", "FALSE"] / (tab["FALSE", "TRUE"] * tab["TRUE", "FALSE"])
print(c(counted_allele_column = names(x)[7], carrier_odds_ratio = carrier_or))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.1", paste0(report, ".raw"), parent = "5.7")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --snp 9:96426973:A:G --export A --out results/guided/s6-1_example --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--snp` selects one variant by its exact current ID. `--export A` writes the [dosage](../docs/glossary.md#dosage) of the named allele: the number of copies, 0, 1 or 2, with missing values kept separate. R then builds the 2-by-2 carrier table. `--pfile` reads the final genotype files. `--out` sets the prefix of the report files. `--threads 2` limits PLINK to two worker threads. `--memory 2048` gives PLINK 2048 MiB (about 2 GB) of working memory.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

A table of carriers and non-carriers in the retained cohort, and a finite odds ratio. Read the direction of the odds ratio with the allele in the exported column. This allele is not always the one that raises risk.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

An OR of 2 means that the probability of disease doubled. Is this statement generally correct?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Odds and probability are different things. An odds ratio is usually not the same as a risk ratio.

</details>

### Files created

`s6-1_example.raw` and the log files.

## 6.2 The additive logistic model {#step-6-2}

### What we do

Fit a [logistic regression](../docs/glossary.md#logistic-regression) for one variant in R. Connect the dosage to the odds ratio.

### Why

Logistic regression suits an outcome with two values, here case or control. It models log(p/(1-p)) = intercept + beta * dosage. Here p is the probability of being a case, and beta is the effect of each extra copy of the allele. An [additive model](../docs/glossary.md#additive-model) assumes that each extra copy changes the log odds by the same amount. exp(beta) is the odds ratio per copy of the allele. It differs from the carrier odds ratio at 6.1. The [standard error](../docs/glossary.md#standard-error) shows how uncertain the estimate of the log odds ratio is. This example uses one variant and no adjustment. It is not the final association result.

### You need

The one-variant export from 6.1 and the final PSAM file (the table of samples).

### Command

```{r s6-2}
x <- read.table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "6.1", "example"), ".raw"), header = TRUE, check.names = FALSE)
psam <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), ".psam"))
example <- data.frame(case = as.numeric(psam$Disease[match(x$IID, psam$IID)] == "2"), dosage = as.numeric(x[[7]]))
fit <- glm(case ~ dosage, data = example, family = binomial())
summary(fit)
exp(coef(fit)["dosage"])
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable. This step needs no PLINK operation. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the values it shows. It does not change the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

An intercept and a dosage coefficient, each with a standard error and a [p-value](../docs/glossary.md#p-value). The odds ratio per allele and the carrier odds ratio need not be equal.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

What does beta = 0 imply for the per-allele odds ratio?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

exp(0) = 1. The estimate shows no change in the odds for each extra copy of the allele.

</details>

### Files created

The example model exists only in R memory. The genotype export from 6.1 stays on disk.

## 6.3 Prepare covariates {#step-6-3}

### What we do

Join age and ten principal components ([PCs](../docs/glossary.md#pca-pc)) to the IDs of the retained samples. Then check that no value is missing and that the table has full rank (explained below).

### Why

Covariates are extra measured factors, such as age. They adjust the comparison between cases and controls. PCs describe ancestry differences between people. If the covariates belong to the wrong samples, every test is wrong, yet the output still looks normal. A sample with a missing covariate is dropped from the model. [Collinearity](../docs/glossary.md#collinearity) means that one column can be predicted exactly from the other columns. Then the model cannot give a single answer. Full rank means that no column has this problem. We check the IDs and the rank before the scan. PLINK reads sex from the PSAM file and adds it to the model.

### You need

The state saved at 5.7, the cohort eigenvectors (the PC values of each sample) from 5.7 and the metadata from 2.7.

### Command

```{r s6-3}
psam <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), ".psam"))
pcs <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "pca"), ".eigenvec"))
metadata <- guided_metadata(cfg)
a <- match(psam$IID, metadata$IID); b <- match(psam$IID, pcs$IID)
stopifnot(!anyNA(a), !anyNA(b), !anyDuplicated(pcs$IID))
covar <- data.frame(FID = psam$FID, IID = psam$IID, Age = as.numeric(metadata$Age[a]))
for (name in paste0("PC", 1:10)) covar[[name]] <- as.numeric(pcs[[name]][b])
stopifnot(!anyNA(covar))
design <- model.matrix(~ ., data = data.frame(SEX = as.numeric(psam$SEX), covar[, -(1:2)]))
stopifnot(qr(design)$rank == ncol(design))
names(covar)[1] <- "#FID"
guided_write(covar, guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "covariates.tsv"))
cat(nrow(covar), "complete covariate rows written\n")
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.3", guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "covariates.tsv"), parent = "6.1")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable. This step needs no PLINK operation. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the values it shows. It does not change the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

1,811 complete covariate rows that match the samples, with Age and PC1 to PC10. There are no duplicate or unmatched IDs. The design has full column rank.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Why is a complete covariate table with the right number of rows not enough by itself?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

The rows must belong to the correct sample IDs. Each row must match its own sample.

</details>

### Files created

`s6-3_covariates.tsv`.

## 6.4 Run the association scan {#step-6-4}

### What we do

Fit the additive logistic model, planned in advance, at every retained variant that PLINK can analyse. The model includes age, sex and ten PCs.

### Why

The scan tests one variant at a time. The covariates stay the same for every test. The [null hypothesis](../docs/glossary.md#null-hypothesis) of the additive test is beta = 0, which means no effect. A small p-value is evidence against the null hypothesis, if the model and its assumptions are right. It does not measure the size of the effect. It does not prove a cause. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Firth fallback means that PLINK switches to Firth correction when the ordinary fit fails, which gives a more stable result. The ordinary fit can fail because of [separation](../docs/glossary.md#separation). We never choose the covariates after we look at the peaks in the results.

### You need

The final genotype files from 5.7 and the covariates from 6.3.

### Command

```{r s6-4}
out <- guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--maf", "0.01", "--covar", guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "covariates.tsv"),
  "--covar-name", "Age,PC1-PC10", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "sex", "hide-covar", "firth-fallback", "--out", out))
results <- guided_association(out)
valid <- valid_p(results$P)
stopifnot(sum(valid) == 236815L, sum(results$P[valid] < 5e-8) == 8L)
guided_write(results, guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "results.tsv"))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.4", c(paste0(out, ".Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid"), guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "results.tsv")), parent = "6.3")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --maf 0.01 --covar results/guided/s6-3_covariates.tsv --covar-name Age,PC1-PC10 --covar-variance-standardize --glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback --out results/guided/s6-4_association --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--maf 0.01` checks the frequency rule again in the final cohort. `--covar` loads the covariate table, which is keyed by sample ID. `--covar-name` selects Age and PC1 to PC10. `--covar-variance-standardize` rescales the numerical covariates so that the fit is stable. It does not change the genetic hypothesis that is tested. `--glm sex` adds the recorded sex to the model. `hide-covar` reports only the genetic tests, not the coefficient of every covariate. `firth-fallback` uses Firth correction when it is needed. `--pfile` reads the final genotype files. `--out` sets the prefix of the report files. `--threads 2` limits PLINK to two worker threads. `--memory 2048` gives PLINK 2048 MiB (about 2 GB) of working memory.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The frequency check in the final cohort removes another 1,698 variants. This leaves 236,815 additive p-values that are finite numbers. Eight of them are below 0.00000005. A variant kept before the scan can still fail the frequency check after the cohort changes. Read the output and the log. Never replace a missing result with zero.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Does a tiny p-value imply a large odds ratio?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. The p-value depends on the effect, the uncertainty and the sample size. Also report the effect estimate and its interval.

</details>

### Files created

`s6-4_association.Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid`, the log files and `s6-4_results.tsv`, a cleaned copy of the results.

## 6.5 Read association output {#step-6-5}

### What we do

Find the effect allele, the sample count, the uncertainty, the type of test and the fitting status in the output.

### Why

A1 is the [effect allele](../docs/glossary.md#effect-allele): the allele whose dosage is tested. It is not automatically the ALT allele, the minor allele or the harmful allele. OR is the odds ratio. It shows how much each copy of A1 multiplies the odds of disease. OBS_CT is the number of samples used at that variant. It can change from variant to variant because of missing calls. ERRCODE describes model failures. A missing p-value must stay missing. A 95% [confidence interval](../docs/glossary.md#ci) is exp(log(OR) +/- 1.96 * SE), where SE is the standard error. This formula is an approximation. The interval shows how uncertain the estimate is, if the assumptions hold. It does not give the chance that this one interval contains the true value.

### You need

The full association output from 6.4.

### Command

```{r s6-5}
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association"))
print(table(results$ERRCODE, useNA = "ifany"))
valid <- results[valid_p(results$P), ]
valid$CI_LOW <- exp(log(valid$OR) - 1.96 * valid[["LOG(OR)_SE"]])
valid$CI_HIGH <- exp(log(valid$OR) + 1.96 * valid[["LOG(OR)_SE"]])
top <- valid[order(valid$P), c("CHROM", "POS", "ID", "A1", "OBS_CT", "OR", "CI_LOW", "CI_HIGH", "P")]
print(head(top, 10))
guided_write(head(top, 20), guided_path(cfg, "6.5", "top20.tsv"))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.5", guided_path(cfg, "6.5", "top20.tsv"), parent = "6.4")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable. This step needs no PLINK operation. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the values it shows. It does not change the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The leading regions are on chromosomes 9, 3 and 12. The table keeps the effect allele and the OBS_CT of each variant. Every p-value and odds ratio refers to the tested A1 allele, whatever the variant ID looks like.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

What should you do with a row that has an ERRCODE for a failure and a missing p-value?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Read the reason for the failure. Keep the p-value as missing. Do not replace it with a number, whether significant or not.

</details>

### Files created

`s6-5_top20.tsv`, with the effect estimates and their intervals.

## 6.6 Sparse genotypes and Firth correction {#step-6-6}

### What we do

Compare an ordinary fit with a Firth fit that we force at one low-frequency autosomal variant. The variant is one of the retained variants.

### Why

A rare genotype can have very few cases or controls. The ordinary logistic fit uses [maximum likelihood](../docs/glossary.md#maximum-likelihood). It chooses the coefficients that make the observed outcomes most likely under the model. Sometimes one genotype group contains only cases or only controls. This is separation, and the coefficient can then grow without limit. [Firth correction](../docs/glossary.md#firth-regression) reduces the bias of small samples and can give finite estimates. It does not add information. It does not fix confounding, wrong genotype calls or a poor study design. The main scan of this dataset did not need the Firth fallback. We force Firth here so that you can compare the two results at one variant. Variants below the 1% frequency filter do not come back.

### You need

The final cohort, the main results from 6.4 and the covariates from 6.3.

### Command

```{r s6-6}
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association"))
minor <- pmin(results$A1_FREQ, 1 - results$A1_FREQ)
candidates <- which(results$CHROM %in% as.character(1:22) & valid_p(results$P) & minor > 0)
chosen <- results$ID[candidates[which.min(minor[candidates])]]
guided_list(chosen, guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "variant.txt"))
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--snp", chosen, "--covar", guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "covariates.tsv"),
  "--covar-name", "Age,PC1-PC10", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "firth", "sex", "hide-covar", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "firth")))
comparison <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "firth"))
print(results[results$ID == chosen, c("ID", "A1", "OR", "P")])
print(comparison[, c("ID", "A1", "OR", "P")])
stopifnot(nrow(comparison) == 1L, valid_p(comparison$P))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --extract results/guided/s6-6_variant.txt --covar results/guided/s6-3_covariates.tsv --covar-name Age,PC1-PC10 --covar-variance-standardize --glm firth sex hide-covar --out results/guided/s6-6_firth --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

The R command uses `--snp` with the chosen ID. The terminal command uses `--extract` with a file that holds this one ID. `--glm firth` asks for Firth correction at this variant, without waiting for the fallback. The covariate options and the resource options are the same as at 6.4. `--pfile` reads the final genotype files. `--out` sets the prefix of the report files. `--threads 2` limits PLINK to two worker threads. `--memory 2048` gives PLINK 2048 MiB (about 2 GB) of working memory.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

One forced Firth result with a finite value, next to the ordinary estimate from the main scan for the same A1 allele. Small differences in the numbers are normal. Forced Firth is not a better scan for the whole genome.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Does Firth correction make an association precise when it rests on very few carriers?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. It makes the fit more stable, but the uncertainty can stay large.

</details>

### Files created

The chosen variant ID, the forced Firth report and the log files.

<details><summary>Under the hood & literature</summary>

**What the tool computes.** Ordinary logistic regression chooses the coefficients that maximise the likelihood. Firth regression subtracts a penalty from it, which removes the leading term of the small-sample bias and keeps the estimates finite. When one genotype group holds only cases or only controls, the ordinary estimate does not exist. The report gives `OR` (the exponential of the coefficient for the `A1` allele), its standard error, the Z statistic and `P`. PLINK 2 reports an asymptotic p-value from the Wald Z statistic, also for Firth fits.

**Why these values.** The main scan used `firth-fallback`, PLINK's default, which switches to Firth only when the ordinary fit fails. We force `firth` once so you can compare. The 1% frequency filter keeps the rarest variants out of the scan.

**Pitfalls.** Firth shrinks estimates towards no effect and gives no new information. With few carriers the Wald p-value can mislead. Penalised likelihood ratio tests and profile confidence intervals are often preferable to the Wald test. For low-count variants (roughly fewer than 400 minor alleles), simulations favour a Firth test over the plain Wald, score or likelihood ratio tests in joint analysis. Always look at the carrier counts and doubt genotype calls at rare variants. The spelling `--covar-variance-standardize` is American; the course text says standardise.

**References**

1. Firth D (1993) Bias reduction of maximum likelihood estimates. Biometrika 80:27-38. doi:10.1093/biomet/80.1.27.
2. Albert A, Anderson JA (1984) On the existence of maximum likelihood estimates in logistic regression models. Biometrika 71:1-10. doi:10.1093/biomet/71.1.1.
3. Heinze G, Schemper M (2002) A solution to the problem of separation in logistic regression. Stat Med 21:2409-2419. PMID 12210625.
4. Ma C et al. (2013) Recommended joint and meta-analysis strategies for case-control association testing of single low-count variants. Genet Epidemiol 37:539-550. PMID 23788246.

</details>

## 6.7 First look and association checkpoint {#step-6-7}

### What we do

Summarise the valid tests. Save the key association files so that you can restart from here.

### Why

A list of small p-values is not yet an interpretation. Before you plot, write down the model, the cohort, the number of tests and the fitting status. The next module explains [multiple testing](../docs/glossary.md#multiple-testing), correlated peaks and confounding. Never call a simulated top result a clinical finding. Never assume that the nearest gene is the cause.

### You need

The association output from 6.4 and the table you reviewed at 6.5.

### Command

```{r s6-7}
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association"))
summary <- data.frame(samples = 1811, retained_variants = 238513, finite_tests = sum(valid_p(results$P)),
  genome_wide = sum(results$P[valid_p(results$P)] < 5e-8),
  lambda_autosomes = lambda_gc(results$P[results$CHROM %in% as.character(1:22)]))
guided_write(summary, guided_path(cfg, "6.7", "summary.tsv"))
print(summary)
files <- c(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association"), ".Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid"),
  guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "covariates.tsv"), guided_path(cfg, "6.5", "top20.tsv"), guided_path(cfg, "6.7", "summary.tsv"))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.7", files)
check_step("6.7", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable. This step needs no PLINK operation. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the values it shows. It does not change the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

1,811 retained samples, 238,513 retained variants and 236,815 tests with finite p-values. Eight variants are genome-wide significant. The autosomal [lambda](../docs/glossary.md#lambda-gc) is about 1.016. The key analysis files get a manifest: a list of files with their [SHA-256](../docs/glossary.md#sha-256) checksums.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Do eight significant variants always mean eight independent association signals?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Nearby variants can share one signal because of [LD](../docs/glossary.md#ld). Clumping at 7.5 groups the correlated associations.

</details>

### Files created

`s6-7_summary.tsv`, the association checkpoint files and `checkpoints/6.7/MANIFEST.tsv`.

## 6.8 Create the summary statistics file {#step-6-8}

### What we do

Save the results of the association scan in one clearly named file with standard columns. Write a second file that explains every column in plain words.

### Why

The raw PLINK output is long and uses PLINK column names. A summary statistics file is the standard way to share GWAS results. It has one row for each tested variant and no data about individual people. Colleagues use it to plot results, to combine several studies into one analysis (a meta-analysis) and to look up a variant. This file keeps only the eleven columns that others expect, with the same names in the same order. From now on we build the [Manhattan plot](../docs/glossary.md#manhattan-plot) and the [QQ plot](../docs/glossary.md#qq-plot) from this file, not from the raw scan output.

Each column has one clear meaning. Read the table before you use the file.

| Column | What it is | What values look like | A common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `chromosome` | The chromosome of the variant. | `1` to `22`, then `X`, `Y` or `MT`. | Treating it as a number. `X` is text. |
| `base_pair_location` | The position on the chromosome, in base pairs, on genome build [GRCh38](../docs/glossary.md#grch38). | A whole number such as `96426973`. | Comparing it with positions from another genome build. |
| `variant_id` | The name of the variant in this course. | `9:96426973:A:G`: chromosome, position and the two alleles. | Expecting an rs number. This course does not use rs numbers as identifiers. |
| `effect_allele` | The allele whose copies the model counted. PLINK calls it A1. | One letter, such as `A`. | Assuming it is the minor allele or the ALT allele. By definition it is neither. |
| `other_allele` | The other allele of the variant. | One letter, such as `G`. | Swapping the two alleles. The odds ratio then points the other way. |
| `effect_allele_frequency` | How common the effect allele is in the analysed samples. | A number from 0 to 1, such as `0.2`. | Reading it as the minor allele frequency ([MAF](../docs/glossary.md#maf)). It can be above 0.5. |
| `odds_ratio` | The odds ratio per copy of the effect allele. | A positive number. Above 1 means higher odds of disease with each copy. | Reading it as a risk ratio. |
| `beta` | The natural logarithm of the odds ratio. It is the effect size on the log odds scale. | A number that can be negative, zero or positive, such as `0.18`. Above 0 means higher odds of disease. It is `NA` when the odds ratio is `NA`. | Mixing it up with the odds ratio. `beta` is `log(odds_ratio)`. An odds ratio of 1 gives a `beta` of 0. |
| `standard_error` | The standard error of `beta`, the natural logarithm of the odds ratio. | A small positive number, such as `0.09`. | Using it as the standard error of the odds ratio itself. It belongs to `beta`. |
| `p_value` | The p-value of the additive test. | A number above 0 and at most 1. A test that failed is `NA`. | Replacing `NA` with 1 or 0. A missing result stays missing. |
| `n` | The number of samples used for this variant. | A whole number up to 1,811. | Assuming every variant uses all samples. Missing genotypes lower it. |

To get the 95% confidence interval of an odds ratio, use `exp(beta +/- 1.96 * standard_error)`. The standard error is on the log scale, so the formula starts from `beta`, the logarithm of the odds ratio.

The file is plain text with a header row. Tabs separate the columns. It uses UTF-8 encoding (a standard way to store text characters) and decimal points. It holds only results for each variant. It has no genotypes and no sample IDs. Even so, it stays in your `results` folder. Do not share it outside the course unless your instructor says so.

### You need

The association scan from 6.4 and the summary from 6.7.

### Command

```{r s6-8}
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association"))
stats <- guided_standardise_scan(results)
guided_check_summary(stats, rows = nrow(results))
stats_file <- guided_summary_path(cfg)
guided_write_summary(stats, stats_file)
dictionary_file <- guided_path(cfg, "6.8", "gwas_summary_statistics_columns.tsv")
guided_write(guided_summary_dictionary(), dictionary_file)
# Read the file back, as the plots will, and check that nothing was lost.
saved <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
guided_check_summary(saved, rows = nrow(results))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(saved, stats)))
first_summary <- read.delim(guided_path(cfg, "6.7", "summary.tsv"))
finite <- valid_p(saved$p_value)
stopifnot(sum(finite) == first_summary$finite_tests, sum(saved$p_value[finite] < 5e-8) == first_summary$genome_wide)
print(head(saved, 5))
print(c(rows = nrow(saved), finite_tests = sum(finite), missing_p_values = sum(is.na(saved$p_value)),
  genome_wide = sum(saved$p_value[finite] < 5e-8)))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.8", c(stats_file, dictionary_file), parent = "6.7")
check_step("6.8", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable. This step needs no PLINK operation. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the values it shows. It does not change the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

The summary statistics file has 236,815 rows, one for each tested variant. It has the eleven columns in the order of the table above. The checks stop the step with an error if a column name, a p-value or an odds ratio breaks the rules. The first row is `1:858952:G:A`, with effect allele `A`, other allele `G`, odds ratio 1.03471, `beta` about 0.034 and n = 1807. `beta` is calculated from the odds ratio that PLINK writes, so it is the logarithm of that rounded value. No p-value is missing in this dataset. Eight p-values are below 0.00000005, as at 6.7. The file is about 22 MB. The column file has one row for each of the eleven columns. The last table shows `matches` for both files in the 6.8 checkpoint.

If PLINK could not calculate a p-value, the file would show `NA`. It would never show 0 or 1.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. If R says that the scan output is missing, run step 6.4 first. If a check names a column or a value, do not edit the file by hand. Run the step again. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

A colleague wants the 95% confidence interval for an odds ratio. Which column do they use with `beta`, and on which scale?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

They use `standard_error`. It is the standard error of `beta`, the natural logarithm of the odds ratio. They calculate the interval on the log scale and then convert it back with `exp()`.

</details>

### Files created

In the folder `results/guided/`: `s6-8_gwas_summary_statistics.tsv` (the summary statistics file), `s6-8_gwas_summary_statistics_columns.tsv` (the column dictionary) and `checkpoints/6.8/MANIFEST.tsv`.

## Module 6 recap {#module-6-recap}

- You calculated a carrier odds ratio by hand and compared it with the odds ratio per allele from a logistic regression.
- You built a covariate table for 1,811 samples with age and PC1 to PC10, and checked it.
- You ran the association scan. The frequency check removed another 1,698 variants, which left 236,815 tests with finite p-values.
- Eight variants had a p-value below 0.00000005. The leading regions are on chromosomes 9, 3 and 12.
- The autosomal lambda is about 1.016.
- You saved the results in a summary statistics file with eleven columns and a file that explains each column.

**Next:** Module 7 draws the QQ plot and the Manhattan plot, sets the thresholds, groups the correlated signals and reports the results.
